Nickel can also be released from materials made of nickel in contact with foods (migration is higher in the case of acidic foods or
foods with citric or acetic acid) (Gil and Gisbert-Calabuig, 2018).
Permissible intakes
The recommended dietary allowances for nickel have not been established but, estimated maximum guideline set by US FDA for Ni
is 70–80 mg/g. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) estimated the tolerable daily intake of nickel from any food source at
2.8 mg/kg body weight, which is 196 mg for an adult and 56 mg for a child. It also determined the Benchmark Dose Lower Conﬁdence
Limit (BMDL10) associated with dermatitis at 1.1 mg/kg body weight. There are currently no maximum levels in EU legislation for Ni
in food nor in the Codex Alimentarius. For natural mineral water a limit of 0.02 mg/L has been established in the Codex (Gil et al.,
2017).
Toxicokinetics
Nickel present in food is poorly absorbed (less than 5–10%) through the gastrointestinal tract probably due to the competition with
various food components (phosphates, phytates, ﬁbers, etc.) that would reduce such absorption. However, absorption is higher
through drinking water (30–40%). Once absorbed, it is distributed in the blood and stored mainly in the kidneys, and also in
